key_insight: Longitudinal oncology retrieval should allocate limited evidence across time rather than repeatedly retrieve similar passages, but the benefit of temporal allocation alone remains unproven.
clinical_relevance: This retrieval research—not a drug discovery study—could help surface treatment changes and recurrences in oncology records, without establishing clinical accuracy.
method: Separate temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.
Compare temporal retrieval with a global baseline using two-stage reconstruction.
Test precedence rules and temporal coverage under fixed evidence budgets.
evidence_signal: Across 13 queries and 20 patient records, Temporal-15 achieved milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for Global-50, but retrieved 496 versus 50 indexed units per query.
watch_item: Unequal retrieval budgets confound the recall gain, and absent expert reference timelines, results measure retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy.
paper_title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
